title: Right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25)
hookLine: the book ends: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes"

cards: Here is the last verse of the book of Judges: "In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes." No song, no victory, no wedding.

The chapters before it are hard to read: a private shrine with a hired priest, a tribe that carries off that shrine's idols and its priest, a crime in a city at night, and a war between the tribes that nearly wipes one of them out.
Then that sentence, like a door closing.

teach.h: NO KING IN ISRAEL: A REFRAIN.
teach.b: The line has been coming back in those last chapters like a refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel.
And the full sentence, everyone doing what was right in his own eyes, stands at both ends of those chapters, as they open, and as the very last line. The phrase has a history.

teach.h: DEUTERONOMY: NOT IN YOUR OWN EYES.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people that in the land they will not do as they do now, every man whatever is right in his own eyes. Instead, the Torah says, do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord.
Same words, other eyes. There's an echo inside Judges too.

teach.h: SAMSON: SHE IS RIGHT IN MY EYES.
teach.b: When Samson first wants a Philistine woman, he tells his father, get her for me, and in Hebrew what he says is: she is right in my eyes.
The man who went after his eyes, in a book that ends with everyone doing what was right in their own. What does the closing line want? Readers differ.

teach.h: A KING, OR GOD AS KING?
teach.b: Some hear a call for a king, and the next book brings one. Others remember that Gideon refused a crown, saying the Lord shall rule over you, and hear the problem as people with no one to answer to but themselves.
Either way, in its telling, a person's own eyes are real, and they matter, but they are not enough by themselves.

how: Jews read the closing verse of Judges as the hinge into the books of Samuel, and commentators differ on whether it calls for a human king or laments a people who no longer answered to God.

o: a time when Israel was ruled directly by its priests
a time when the tribes chose a new leader each year
a time when everyone did what was right in their own eyes

s: the book of Judges ends with a victory song
it ends: there was no king in Israel; every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Samson's words about the Philistine woman are, in Hebrew, 'she is right in my eyes'
the same phrase the book closes with.

games.q: the book of Judges is closing. after a run of dark stories, what's the last line?
o: a song of thanks for the judges.
there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes.
a list of the tribes at peace.
games.why: the book ends on the refrain, unresolved, and leaves the question open for the books of Samuel.

practice: Pick one habit you'd defend if anyone asked, how you spend the evening, how you talk when you're tired, and look at it through your own eyes first.
Then look through the eyes of someone it affects, and, if you have one, through the eyes of your tradition, without changing anything yet.

wordCard.voice: no king. The refrain of Judges' last chapters, about a time when everyone answered only to their own eyes.

orig.note: Hebrew: what is right in his eyes, the closing words of the book of Judges.
